plain_cards.front: AIA A101 covers what agreement and pricing basis?
plain_cards.back: Owner–Contractor agreement where basis of payment is a Stipulated Sum (Lump Sum). Incorporates A201 General Conditions.

plain_cards.front: AIA A102 vs. A103: what is the difference?
plain_cards.back: Both are Owner–Contractor Cost of the Work Plus a Fee; A102 includes a Guaranteed Maximum Price (GMP), A103 has no GMP.

plain_cards.front: AIA A133 covers which delivery method?
plain_cards.back: Owner–Construction Manager as Constructor (CMaR) where basis of payment is Cost of the Work Plus a Fee with a GMP (preconstruction + construction).

plain_cards.front: AIA A141 covers which delivery method?
plain_cards.back: Owner–Design-Builder agreement (single contract holding both design and construction responsibility).

plain_cards.front: AIA A201 is the keystone document for what?
plain_cards.back: General Conditions of the Contract for Construction — defines rights, responsibilities, and relationships of Owner, Contractor, and Architect during construction.

plain_cards.front: AIA A305 is used during bidding for what purpose?
plain_cards.back: Contractor's Qualification Statement — vets bidder financial stability, bonding capacity, experience, and prior litigation before bidding/award.

plain_cards.front: AIA A310 vs. A312: which bonds are which?
plain_cards.back: A310 = Bid Bond (guarantees bidder will enter contract if awarded). A312 = Performance Bond + Payment Bond (guarantees completion & sub/supplier payment).

plain_cards.front: AIA B101 covers what agreement?
plain_cards.back: Standard Owner–Architect Agreement for basic services (SD, DD, CD, Bidding, CA), supplemental/additional services, compensation, and instruments of service.

plain_cards.front: AIA C401 covers what agreement?
plain_cards.back: Architect–Consultant Agreement (e.g., structural, MEP, civil) — flows down B101 prime-agreement obligations ('conduit' / pass-through).

plain_cards.front: AIA G701 is what construction administration form?
plain_cards.back: Change Order — modifies Contract Sum and/or Contract Time; requires ALL THREE signatures: Owner, Architect, and Contractor.

plain_cards.front: AIA G702 and G703 are used for what?
plain_cards.back: G702 = Application and Certificate for Payment (certified by Architect). G703 = Continuation Sheet / Schedule of Values itemizing % complete per line.

plain_cards.front: AIA G704 certifies what milestone, and what starts on that date?
plain_cards.back: Certificate of Substantial Completion — project is sufficiently complete for intended occupancy; starts warranty periods, transfers insurance/utilities to Owner, and triggers punch list.

plain_cards.front: AIA G706 & G706A protect the Owner from what at closeout?
plain_cards.back: G706 = Contractor's Affidavit of Payment of Debts & Claims; G706A = Affidavit of Release of Liens — protects Owner against mechanics' liens before final payment.

plain_cards.front: AIA G707 is required before final payment when a project is bonded — what is it?
plain_cards.back: Consent of Surety to Final Payment — ensures the surety agrees to release retainage/final payment without voiding bond coverage.

plain_cards.front: AIA G710 (ASI) does what — and what can it NOT change?
plain_cards.back: Architect's Supplemental Instructions — clarifies drawings or makes minor changes ONLY if they involve NO change in Contract Sum and NO change in Contract Time.

plain_cards.front: AIA G714 (CCD) differs from a G701 Change Order how?
plain_cards.back: Construction Change Directive — directs work when Owner & Contractor haven't agreed on cost/time; signed by Owner + Architect only (no Contractor signature required to start work).

plain_cards.front: Under AIA B101 §2.2, why must an architect reject 'highest standard' or 'warranty' wording?
plain_cards.back: E&O insurance covers only ordinary negligence against the local professional Standard of Care; warranties or 'best/highest' promises create uninsured contractual liability.

plain_cards.front: Under AIA B101, who owns copyright to the Instruments of Service?
plain_cards.back: The Architect (and consultants) retain copyright; upon payment, the Owner receives a nonexclusive license solely for constructing, using, and maintaining the project.

plain_cards.front: AIA B101 & A201 include a Mutual Waiver of Consequential Damages — what does it exclude?
plain_cards.back: Indirect/downstream losses (lost rent, lost profits, financing penalties, reputational harm); parties limit claims to direct damages or agreed liquidated damages.

plain_cards.front: What is the default dispute-resolution sequence under AIA A201?
plain_cards.back: Initial Decision Maker (default: Architect) → Mediation (mandatory condition precedent) → Binding Dispute Resolution (Arbitration or Litigation, selected in agreement).

plain_cards.front: Under A201, who is solely responsible for construction means, methods, techniques, and jobsite safety?
plain_cards.back: The Contractor — never the Architect. Directing jobsite safety or construction methods transfers liability to the Architect.

plain_cards.front: Can the Architect stop construction work if they spot nonconforming work or an unsafe scaffold?
plain_cards.back: NO. Only the Owner can issue a stop-work order (A201 §2.4). The Architect has authority to REJECT nonconforming work and notify the Owner/Contractor in writing.

plain_cards.front: What is the Architect's scope when reviewing shop drawings and submittals?
plain_cards.back: Limited to checking conformance with information given and design concept expressed in the Contract Documents — NOT verifying field dimensions, quantities, or safety.

plain_cards.front: Are approved shop drawings / submittals considered Contract Documents under A201?
plain_cards.back: NO. Approved submittals do not modify the Contract Documents; any deviation requires a formal modification (CO, CCD, or ASI).

plain_cards.front: What is an RFI (Request for Information) vs. an ASI?
plain_cards.back: RFI = Contractor asks Architect to clarify ambiguities/conflicts in CDs (no cost/time change). ASI = Architect proactively issues minor clarification/change (no cost/time change).

plain_cards.front: When is a Proposal Request (PR / AIA G709) issued?
plain_cards.back: When the Owner/Architect contemplates a change affecting cost or time and wants a Contractor price/schedule quote BEFORE authorizing work via Change Order.

plain_cards.front: Under A201, how many days does the Architect have to certify (or withhold) a Contractor's G702 pay app?
plain_cards.back: 7 days after receipt (either certify for payment or notify Contractor and Owner in writing of reasons for withholding).

plain_cards.front: Can a Contractor bill for materials stored off-site on a G702 pay application?
plain_cards.back: Only with prior Owner approval plus proof of title/bill of sale, proper storage/identification, and insurance covering the off-site location.

plain_cards.front: What makes Liquidated Damages enforceable vs. an unenforceable penalty?
plain_cards.back: Must be a reasonable pre-estimate of hard-to-quantify daily Owner delay losses agreed at contract signing — cannot be punitive. Often paired with early-completion bonus.

plain_cards.front: Addendum vs. Change Order: when is each issued?
plain_cards.back: Addendum modifies Bidding Documents BEFORE contract award (issued to all bidders). Change Order modifies Contract Documents AFTER contract execution.

plain_cards.front: Bid Alternate vs. Allowance vs. Unit Price?
plain_cards.back: Alternate = optional scope priced separately at bid. Allowance = placeholder dollar sum for an unspecified item (reconciled later). Unit Price = fixed rate per quantity (e.g., $/CY rock removal).

plain_cards.front: Who prepares the initial Punch List before Substantial Completion under A201?
plain_cards.back: The Contractor prepares the comprehensive list of items to be completed/corrected; the Architect then inspects and adds any omitted items before issuing G704.

plain_cards.front: What is the standard A201 one-year Correction of Work period vs. general warranty?
plain_cards.back: Contractor must promptly correct defective work within 1 year after Substantial Completion (obligation to return); general warranty/statute of limitations can extend longer.

plain_cards.front: What is a Mechanic's Lien and how do Owners prevent it?
plain_cards.back: Statutory security interest filed against real property by an unpaid contractor/sub/supplier. Prevented via conditional/unconditional lien waivers with pay apps and payment bonds.

plain_cards.front: Who typically carries Builder's Risk (property) insurance during construction under A201?
plain_cards.back: The Owner (covering full insurable replacement value of work-in-progress against fire/theft/weather), while the Contractor carries Commercial General Liability (CGL) & Workers' Comp.

plain_cards.front: CSI MasterFormat: what is in Division 00 vs. Division 01?
plain_cards.back: Division 00 = Procurement & Contracting Requirements (bidding, agreements, A201). Division 01 = General Requirements (submittals, closeout, quality control, temporary facilities).

plain_cards.front: CSI MasterFormat key technical divisions: 03, 05, 07, 08, 09, 23, 26?
plain_cards.back: 03 Concrete, 05 Metals, 07 Thermal & Moisture Protection, 08 Openings (doors/windows), 09 Finishes, 23 HVAC, 26 Electrical.

plain_cards.front: Performance vs. Prescriptive vs. Proprietary specifications?
plain_cards.back: Performance = states required outcome/criteria (contractor picks means). Prescriptive = details exact materials/installation. Proprietary = names exact brand/product (closed or 'or equal').

plain_cards.front: Under A201, if drawings and specifications conflict, which takes precedence?
plain_cards.back: Neither automatically — Contract Documents are complementary! Architect interprets intent; typically more stringent/expensive requirement or specific detail over general governs unless specified otherwise.

plain_cards.front: Design-Bid-Build (DBB): defining feature, biggest pro, biggest con?
plain_cards.back: Separate Owner contracts with Architect and GC; sequential phases. Pro: competitive low-bid price & checks/balances. Con: longest schedule, no contractor preconstruction input, adversarial claims.

plain_cards.front: CM at Risk (CMaR / A133) vs. CM as Adviser (CMa / C132)?
plain_cards.back: CMaR holds trade subcontracts and guarantees a GMP (at financial risk). CMa is a fee-only Owner consultant holding zero trade contracts (Owner holds multiple prime contracts).

plain_cards.front: Design-Build (DB): biggest pro and biggest tradeoff for the Owner?
plain_cards.back: Single point of responsibility + fastest overlapping schedule. Tradeoff: Owner loses independent Architect advocacy/checks-and-balances (bridging architect sometimes hired).

plain_cards.front: Integrated Project Delivery (IPD): what distinguishes it contractually?
plain_cards.back: Single multi-party agreement signed by Owner, Architect, and Contractor sharing risk/reward pool, early involvement of all parties, open-book accounting, and liability waivers among team.

plain_cards.front: Critical Path Method (CPM): what is the Critical Path and what is its Float?
plain_cards.back: Longest sequential chain of dependent activities determining minimum project duration. Every task on the critical path has ZERO Total Float.

plain_cards.front: Free Float vs. Total Float in a CPM schedule?
plain_cards.back: Free Float = delay allowed without delaying the next activity's early start. Total Float = delay allowed without pushing out the final project completion date.

plain_cards.front: What is Fast-Track construction and its main risk?
plain_cards.back: Starting early construction packages (excavation/foundation) before full CDs are complete. Cuts schedule, but raises coordination errors, redesign cost, and late change orders.

plain_cards.front: Firm financial ratio: Net Multiplier formula & healthy range?
plain_cards.back: Net Operating Revenue ÷ Direct Labor Cost. Measures how many dollars of revenue each direct labor dollar generates; healthy architectural firm target ~2.8–3.2 (must exceed Break-Even Rate = 1 + Overhead Rate).

plain_cards.front: Overhead Rate and Break-Even Rate formulas?
plain_cards.back: Overhead Rate = Total Indirect Expenses ÷ Total Direct Labor (typical ~1.3–1.7). Break-Even Rate = 1.0 + Overhead Rate (~2.3–2.7).

plain_cards.front: Real estate pro forma: NOI and Capitalization Rate (Cap Rate) formula?
plain_cards.back: NOI = Effective Gross Income − Operating Expenses (excludes debt service & depreciation). Property Value = NOI ÷ Cap Rate.

plain_cards.front: Project budget: Hard Costs vs. Soft Costs?
plain_cards.back: Hard Costs = physical construction (labor, materials, site work, GC overhead). Soft Costs = design/engineering fees, permits, legal, financing, testing, insurance (~20–30% of total).

plain_cards.front: Design Contingency vs. Construction Contingency?
plain_cards.back: Design Contingency shrinks from ~15–20% in SD to ~0% at bid as scope hardens. Construction Contingency (~5% new build, ~10% renovation) covers unforeseen field conditions/COs.

plain_cards.front: True Value Engineering (VE) vs. simple cost-cutting?
plain_cards.back: VE analyzes life-cycle cost vs. function (achieving equal or better performance at lower total life-cycle cost), not merely slashing initial capital cost by degrading quality.

plain_cards.front: Sole Proprietorship vs. General Partnership vs. LLC vs. Corporation (liability)?
plain_cards.back: Sole Prop & General Partnership = unlimited personal liability (and joint-and-several for partners). LLC / Corp / PC = shields personal assets from firm business debts (never from one's own malpractice).

plain_cards.front: Floor Area Ratio (FAR): formula and what does FAR 4.0 allow on a 10,000 sf lot?
plain_cards.back: FAR = Total Gross Building Floor Area ÷ Net Lot Area. FAR 4.0 on 10,000 sf = 40,000 sf total (e.g., 4 stories × 100% lot, or 8 stories × 50% lot coverage).

plain_cards.front: Zoning Variance vs. Conditional Use Permit (CUP) vs. Rezoning?
plain_cards.back: Variance = relief from dimensional rules (setback/height) proving unique site hardship. CUP = permitted use with extra conditions. Rezoning = legislative change to zoning map/text.

plain_cards.front: Easement vs. Restrictive Covenant (Deed Restriction)?
plain_cards.back: Easement = legal right for another party to use/cross part of land (utility, access, solar). Covenant = private deed restriction limiting use/appearance (stricter of zoning or covenant governs).

plain_cards.front: Environmental Site Assessment: Phase I ESA vs. Phase II ESA?
plain_cards.back: Phase I = non-invasive historical records, site walk, interviews to spot Recognized Environmental Conditions (RECs). Phase II = physical soil/groundwater/asbestos sampling & lab testing if Phase I flags RECs.

plain_cards.front: Brownfield vs. Greyfield vs. Greenfield site?
plain_cards.back: Brownfield = previously developed site with real or perceived environmental contamination. Greyfield = economically obsolete developed site (dead mall/parking lot) without major toxics. Greenfield = undeveloped land.

plain_cards.front: 2010 ADA Standards: max running slope, max cross slope, and max rise per ramp run?
plain_cards.back: 1:12 max running slope (8.33%), 1:48 max cross slope (2.08%), and 30 inches max vertical rise per run before a 60-inch level landing (ADA §405).

plain_cards.front: Why do '5-over-1' buildings dominate US urban infill?
plain_cards.back: IBC §510.2 (podium/horizontal building separation) lets a Type IIIA or VA (sprinklered) building sit above a 3-hour horizontal assembly over a Type IA podium; the 5-story count needs Type IIIA (R-2, NFPA 13: IIIA = 5 stories, VA = 4 per Table 504.4), which is how it maximizes rentable area per dollar.

plain_cards.front: IBC Construction Types I through V ordered from most to least fire-resistive?
plain_cards.back: I = Noncombustible highest fire-resistance (concrete/protected steel); II = Noncombustible lower rating; III = Noncombustible ext. walls + combustible interior; IV = Heavy/Mass Timber; V = Combustible (wood frame). Suffix A = protected, B = unprotected.

plain_cards.front: IBC Occupancy Groups: A, B, E, F, H, I, M, R, S, U?
plain_cards.back: A Assembly, B Business, E Educational, F Factory, H High-Hazard, I Institutional (hospitals/prisons), M Mercantile, R Residential, S Storage, U Utility/Misc.

plain_cards.front: IBC general rule: at what occupant load are two exits required (most occupancies)?
plain_cards.back: ≥50 occupants for Group A, B, E, F, M, U (≥10 for R-2/R-3 stories above 1st; ≥30 for S). When 2 exits are required, separate them by ≥1/2 diagonal (≥1/3 diagonal if fully sprinklered).

plain_cards.front: Northern Hemisphere passive solar rule for South vs. East/West facades?
plain_cards.back: South = high summer sun (easy to shade with horizontal overhangs), low winter sun (passive heat gain). East/West = low-angle harsh sun requiring vertical fins or minimized glazing.

plain_cards.front: Site grading slopes: drainage away from foundation, max accessible walk without ramp, max grass mowing slope?
plain_cards.back: Foundation drainage = min 5% (6 in over first 10 ft). Accessible walkway (not a ramp) = ≤5% (1:20). Comfortable lawn mowing = ≤25–33% (4:1 to 3:1).

plain_cards.front: Topographic contour lines: how do valleys/swales vs. ridges point, and what does close spacing mean?
plain_cards.back: Contours point UPHILL in valleys/swales and DOWNHILL on ridges. Closely spaced contours = steep slope; wide spacing = gentle/flat grade.

plain_cards.front: Heat Island mitigation & passive cooling: albedo, thermal mass, stack ventilation?
plain_cards.back: High-albedo (reflective) surfaces & vegetated roofs cut urban heat island; high thermal mass flattens diurnal swings (hot-arid); stack ventilation vents hot air high and draws cool air low.

plain_cards.front: Why must footings sit below the local frost line, and what happens below the water table?
plain_cards.back: Below frost line prevents frost-heave cracking from freezing soil moisture. Below water table requires hydrostatic waterproofing, dewatering during construction, and uplift/buoyancy resistance.

plain_cards.front: Secretary of the Interior's four treatments for historic properties (most to least conservative)?
plain_cards.back: Preservation (maintain existing form), Rehabilitation (compatible new use while keeping historic character — tax credit eligible), Restoration (return to one specific era), Reconstruction (rebuild vanished structure).
